extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalists or editors interested in 19th-century newspaper practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards—both editorial and business—used to judge or produce U.S. daily and evening newspapers in the late 19th century (circa 1872–1892). Focus is on qualities like news enterprise, independence, sensationalism, pricing, and management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of news as the dominant function
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should prioritize the publication of news as the dominant function (e.g., 'Grady ... always believed in the publication of news as the dominant function of journalism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be an alert, resourceful news-gatherer and rapid, clear writer; scoops and prompt, accurate reporting build reputation (examples: Grady's Florida canvassing-board coverage and Charleston earthquake reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive crusading and exposés
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should pursue crusades and exposures of corruption and local abuses (e.g., McClure attacked the 'city-hall banditti' with incisive boldness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use investigative editorials and reporting to hold power to account; such crusades can win public influence but may provoke libel suits and enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from party or external control
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful paper often prided itself on independence of political control (examples: Post became 'independent in politics'; News 'independent of political control').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain editorial autonomy from parties, advertisers, and politicians to preserve credibility and public trust (Scripps stressed 'it did not allow itself to be influenced by advertisers or politicians').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and limits) of sensationalism and bold headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational headlines and play-up of crime and shocking material were explicit techniques for rapidly increasing circulation (Taylor's Globe and Storey's Times used sensationalism and alliterative/punning headlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensationalism draws readers and can boost circulation quickly, but risks damaging 'cleanliness and tone,' provoking legal trouble, and repelling more decorous audiences; balance sensational copy with decency if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough local coverage and community engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers achieved success through thorough local coverage (e.g., Globe printed thousands of readers' names and emphasized 'thorough local and New England coverage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in local reporting and community features to build a loyal readership; personal touches (naming readers) can strengthen engagement and circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature material and serialized fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of feature material, departmental features, and serials by famous novelists was an attraction (the Globe emphasized feature material with serials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use features and serials to broaden appeal beyond straight news and to increase repeat readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price strategy and penny-paper model
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutting price (two-cent, one-cent papers) and adding editions (evening/morning) were crucial tactics for circulation growth (Taylor cut to two cents; penny papers boomed circulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower unit price to expand audience rapidly; be prepared to scale business/ad revenue to offset lower cover price and to time reductions to stimulate a circulation boom.

rubrics_metrics.name: News enterprise and investigative resourcefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional news enterprise—aggressive pursuit of scoops and detective-style reporting—distinguished leading papers (Stone traced an embezzler from Canada to England; reporters scooped confessions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate reporters capable of field investigation and persistence; exclusive, vividly reported stories raise a paper's national reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial strength, rhetoric, and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful editorial page, often rhetorical and quotable, extended a paper's influence (Watterson's florid, rhetorical editorials were widely copied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop memorable, forceful editorial writing to shape opinion and increase reuse by other papers; rhetorical flourish can be an asset if aligned with credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Business decisions—price cuts, edition changes, reorganizations, capitalization—were determinative of success (Taylor's price cut and new edition; Lawson's business management turning News profitable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine editorial ambition with sound business strategy: capitalization, advertising management, edition planning, and sensible partnerships are critical to survival and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Championing labor and the poor / reform causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some chains and papers explicitly championed labor, unionism, and the interests of the poor and fought bossism (Scripps papers: 'championship of unionism and the interests of the poor', 'war against bossism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear civic stances to mobilize constituencies and define editorial identity; this can attract loyal readers but also create political enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness and tone; avoidance of Bohemian sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's 'cleanliness and tone' was a valued attribute in some markets; Boston prided itself on being comparatively free of the more shocking sensationalism ('Bohemian' was now a rarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards of decorum and tasteful reporting for audiences that value literate, restrained journalism; this differentiates papers in certain markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation as the principal success metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation figures and rank (e.g., 'consolidated circulation', 'passed the 100,000 mark') are repeatedly used to measure a paper's standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and publicize circulation milestones; use circulation growth as evidence of editorial/business success and bargaining power with advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent by-lines and front-page attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of by-lines—even on front page stories—could enhance a reporter's and paper's reputation (Grady's story 'printed with a by-line on the front page ... gave Grady a national reputation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute strong pieces to named reporters to build journalistic star power and reader trust; prominent by-lines can translate into prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building a specialized, brilliant staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruitment of notable writers and critics (humorists, dramatic critics, city editors) contributed to a paper's quality and reputation (Daily News staff included Eugene Field, Amy Leslie, George Harvey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in talent across beats—features, criticism, humor—to produce distinctive content and maintain broad readership appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and fairness in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers strove for impartial reporting even when independent in politics (News described as 'impartial'; many papers moved from party organs to more independent stances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice balanced reporting to sustain credibility among diverse readers; impartiality can coexist with an editorial voice on opinion pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of short, succinct items and readable layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some successful papers specialized in very short items and condensed writing (News specialized in very short items—'often twenty-five or thirty in a single column').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format copy for quick consumption—short items, concise reporting and varied column content—to appeal to mass urban readers with limited time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to litigate and acceptance of legal risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive editorializing and sensational content frequently invited libel suits (McClure 'won twenty libel suits'; Storey acted as defendant in many libel suits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and prepare for legal challenges when engaging in bold exposés or sensational attacks; weigh reputational gains against legal costs and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional stunts and creative circulation marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions and stunts (printing readers' names, firing guns to celebrate circulation, encouraging penny use via merchants marking prices) were used to build readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ creative marketing and community-oriented promotions to spark rapid circulation growth; tailor stunts to local sensibilities to avoid backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial alignment and party decisions as strategic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers' political alignments (bolting parties, supporting candidates) shaped identity and audience (examples: papers bolting Blaine, supporting Cleveland, or deserting party lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit decisions about party alignment and be prepared for audience/advertiser consequences; alignment can mobilize loyal readers or alienate others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion through chains and ownership consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Owning multiple papers and forming chains or leagues was a path to influence and economic scale (Scripps chain beginnings; later Scripps-McRae League).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue measured expansion to create economies of scale and a shared editorial/business philosophy; ensure local relevance in each market to avoid over-centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary and commemorative front-page content
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing full front-page tributes or literary content (e.g., the Globe filled its entire front page with poetical tributes after Garfield's death) was an editorial tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy special-occasion content to demonstrate cultural leadership and solidarity with readers during major events; such choices can enhance prestige but should be used judiciously.
